newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Patten says China's plans bad press for Hong Kong.
newsitem.headline: Patten says China's plans bad press for Hong Kong.

text.p: Hong Kong governor Chris Patten on Tuesday said that verbal sparring over the territory's future did it no lasting damage in international eyes, but Beijing's plans to roll back civil liberties did.

"Hong Kong doesn't have a bad international press because of speeches that are made by people, it has a bad international press -- when it has one -- because of the things that are done or threatened in Hong Kong," Patten told reporters.

Last week, chief executive designate Tung Chee-hwa, who will replace Patten as Hong Kong's leader when the colony reverts to China at midnight on June 30, accused pro-democracy activists of spreading gloom overseas about the future.

"Recently, some well-known people, including the Democratic Party, have blackened the reputation of Hong Kong overseas..., giving the impression that Hong Kong is collapsing," Tung said last Thursday. "This, I feel, is not very good."
The Democratic Party, Hong Kong's largest, has vehemently opposed Beijing's plan to replace the territory's elected legislature and repeal some human rights laws.
Party leader Martin Lee, while visiting Europe this month, urged the European Union to oppose the changes.
Patten said free speech was not a problem as Hong Kong had prospered despite many verbal disagreements over the years.

"I think that what has been a worry in the last few weeks isn't anybody making speeches, I think what has been a worry is some of the decisions announced about the Bill of Rights and about our civil liberties protection," he said.
China insists the changes it wants to make to Hong Kong's Bill of Rights are merely technical and will not curtail freedoms in the territory.
